   Guide to City Council Proceedings

Meetings of the City Council are held the first and third Tuesday of each month at 9:00 a.m. and
are conducted in accordance with Rosenberg's Rules of Order (Vernon Municipal Code Section
2.04.020).

Copies of all agenda items and back-up materials are available for review in the City Clerk
Department, Vernon City Hall, 4305 Santa Fe Avenue, Vernon, California, and are available for
public inspection during regular business hours, Monday through Thursday, 7:00 a.m. to 5:30 p.m.
Agenda reports may be reviewed on the City's website at www.cityofvernon.org or copies may be
purchased for $0.10 per page.

Disability-related services are available to enable persons with a disability to participate in this
meeting, consistent with the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). In compliance with ADA, if you
need special assistance, please contact the City Clerk department at CityClerk@cityofvernon.org or
(323) 583-8811 at least 48 hours prior to the meeting to assure arrangements can be made.

The Public Comment portion of the agenda is for members of the public to present items, which
are not listed on the agenda but are within the subject matter jurisdiction of the City Council. The
City Council cannot take action on any item that is not on the agenda but matters raised under
Public Comment may be referred to staff or scheduled on a future agenda. Comments are limited to
three minutes per speaker unless a different time limit is announced. Speaker slips are available at
the entrance to the Council Chamber.

Public Hearings are legally noticed hearings. For hearings involving zoning matters, the applicant
and appellant will be given 15 minutes to present their position to the City Council. Time may be set
aside for rebuttal. All other testimony shall follow the rules as set for under Public Comment. If you
challenge any City action in court, you may be limited to raising only those issues you or someone
else raised during the public hearing, or in written correspondence delivered to the City Clerk at or
prior to the public hearing.

Consent Calendar items may be approved by a single motion. If a Council Member or the public
wishes to discuss an item, it may be removed from the calendar for individual consideration.
Council Members may indicate a negative or abstaining vote on any individual item by so declaring
prior to the vote on the motion to adopt the Consent Calendar. Items excluded from the Consent
Calendar will be taken up following action on the Consent Calendar. Public speakers shall follow
the guidelines as set forth under Public Comment.

New Business items are matters appearing before the Council for the first time for formal action.
Those wishing to address the Council on New Business items shall follow the guidelines for Public
Comment.

Closed Session allows the Council to discuss specific matters pursuant to the Brown Act,
Government Code Section 54956.9. Based on the advise of the City Attorney, discussion of these
matters in open session would prejudice the position of the City. Following Closed Session, the
City Attorney will provide an oral report on any reportable matters discussed and actions taken. At
the conclusion of Closed Session, the Council may continue any item listed on the Closed Session
agenda to the Open Session agenda for discussion or to take formal action as it deems
appropriate.

Background

Department:  Public Works
Submitted by:  Dulce Gonzalez, Management Analyst

Subject
Arbor Day Proclamation

Recommendation
Proclaim April 22, 2026, as Arbor Day in the City of Vernon.

Background
Arbor Day traces its roots to Nebraska in 1872, when journalist and conservationist J. Sterling
Morton proposed the first celebration, resulting in the planting of over one million trees. Today,
all 50 states recognize Arbor Day as an occasion for environmental stewardship through the
planting, protection, and preservation of urban and rural forests.

The City has steadily expanded its urban forest to improve air quality, enhance the appearance
of our streets and neighborhoods, and promote environmental health. Central to that effort is the
City's ongoing participation in the Tree City USA program, administered by the Arbor Day
Foundation in partnership with the U.S. Forest Service and the National Association of State
Foresters. The program gives communities a structured framework for managing and growing
their public tree canopy.

This year, the City is partnering with the Los Angeles Unified School District and the Los Angeles
Opera to host an Arbor Day celebration on April 22, 2026, at Vernon City Elementary School.
The event will bring together environmental education and the performing arts, giving students
and community members a meaningful experience centered on tree planting and stewardship.

The City is currently pursuing its seventh consecutive Tree City USA designation. To remain
eligible, the City must meet four core standards, one of which is the official proclamation and
observance of Arbor Day by the City Council. Proclaiming April 22, 2026, as Arbor Day satisfies
that requirement and keeps the City on track for its 2026 application. A separate agenda item
covering the formal application submission is scheduled for the June 16, 2026, City Council
meeting.
Fiscal Impact
There is no fiscal impact associated with this report.

Subject
Operating Account Warrant Register

Recommendation
Approve Operating Account Warrant Register No. 171, for the period of March 1, 2026 through
March 21, 2026, totaling $14,795,334.53 and consisting of ratification of electronic payments
totaling $14,102,775.51 and ratification of the issuance of early checks totaling $692,559.02.

Background
Vernon Municipal Code Section 2.32.060 indicates the City Treasurer, or an authorized
designee, shall prepare warrants covering claims or demands against the City which are to be

   City Council Agenda Report

Meeting Date:  April 21, 2026
From:  Genoveva Rocha, City Clerk
Department:  City Clerk
Submitted by:  Sandra Dolson, Deputy City Clerk

Subject
New Regulations for the Discharge of Fats, Oils, and Grease to the City’s Sewer System

Recommendation
A. Find that the proposed action is exempt from the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA)
review, because the adoption of the ordinance is not a “project” pursuant to California Code of
Regulations, Title 14 Section 15378(b)(2) as the Ordinance is a general policy and procedure
making activity; and
B. Adopt Ordinance No. 1312, adding Chapter 13.25 to the Vernon Municipal Code regulating
the discharge of fats, oils, and grease (FOG) to the City’s Sewer System.

Background
During the City Council Meeting on April 7, 2026, the City Council introduced Ordinance No. 1312
by title and waived the requirement of further reading. This ordinance adds Chapter 13.25 to the
Vernon Municipal Code, which regulates the discharge of fats, oils, and grease (FOG) into the
City’s sewer system to comply with State regulatory requirements. The ordinance establishes
operational and discharge standards aimed at preventing sewer blockages and overflows that
could pose significant risks to public health. Additionally, it seeks to avoid regulatory enforcement
and fines from State and Federal agencies, as well as potential third-party liability related to water
quality impacts.

The Summary of the Ordinance was posted on the City’s website on April 7, 2026, and published
on April 9, 2026, pursuant to legal requirements.

Fiscal Impact
There is no fiscal impact associated with this report.

  establish and enforce within its limits all local, police, sanitary, and other
  ordinances and regulations not in conflict with general laws.

B.  California Government Code section 54739 authorizes local agencies to regulate
  the discharge of industrial waste into the public sewer to protect public
  infrastructure, personnel, and the environment including the authority to require
  pretreatment of waste and prohibiting certain discharges.

C.  Sewer overflows are hazardous or injurious to the health, safety, and welfare of
  the general public.

D.  The unregulated discharge of fats, oils, and grease into the City’s sewer system is
  a primary cause of sewer overflows within the City of Vernon.

E.  The City Council desires to regulate the discharge of fats, oils, and grease into the
  City’s sewer system to prevent sanitary sewer overflows and protect public health,
  safety, and welfare, and ensure compliance with applicable state and federal
  requirements.

  CHAPTER 13.25
  FATS, OILS AND GREASE (FOG) REGULATIONS

13.25.010. Title.

This chapter shall be known as the "Fats, Oils and Grease (FOG) Ordinance of the
City of Vernon" (hereinafter "this chapter").

13.25.020. Statutory authority.

The provisions of this chapter are adopted pursuant to the Statewide General Waste
Discharge Requirements for Sanitary Sewer Systems, Water Quality Order No. 2022-
0103-DWQ, Statewide Waste Discharge Requirements General Order for Sanitary
Sewer Systems (SSS WDRs), as adopted by the State Water Board. Nothing in this
chapter prohibits the Director of Public Works and the Director of Health and
Environmental Control, or their designees, from regulating sewers or stormwater in a
manner that exceeds the requirements of the Clean Water Act, the State Water
Resources Control Board, Regional Board, and Los Angeles County Sanitation
District. This chapter is further adopted pursuant to paragraphs (1) and (2) of
subdivision (a) of Government Code section 54739 and is intended to regulate,
prohibit, and control discharges into the City’s sewer system, and to require
pretreatment, monitoring, reporting, and best management practices necessary to
protect the public sewer system and prevent sanitary sewer overflows.

13.25.030. Purpose and intent.

A. The purpose and intent of the provisions in this chapter are to enhance beneficial
  public use of the City’s sewer infrastructure, prevent blockages of sewer lines
  resulting from discharges of fats, oils and grease (FOG) or other constituents to
  the sewer infrastructure and to specify appropriate FOG discharge requirements
  for food service establishments (FSEs).

B. The provisions of this chapter shall apply to the direct and indirect discharge of all
  FOG carried to the City sewer infrastructure.

C. This chapter is established to comply with federal, state, and local regulations
  and standards relating to FOG discharges to the City sewer infrastructure.

D. This chapter establishes quality and quantity standards on all wastewater and/or
  waste discharges containing FOG which may create a blockage, a reduction in
  sewer capacity, and/or cause or contribute to the occurrence of sanitary sewer
  overflows (SSOs).

E. Notwithstanding any other provision of the Municipal Code, enforcement,
  abatement, cost recovery, lien, and special assessment procedures for violations

  involving fats, oils, and grease, sanitary sewer overflows, or grease-related sewer
  damage shall be governed exclusively by this chapter.

13.25.040. Local authority.

The Director of Health and Environmental Control and the Director of Public Works
shall enforce the provisions of this chapter.

13.25.050. Definitions.

A. Unless otherwise defined herein, terms related to water quality shall be as
  adopted in the latest edition of Standard Methods for Examination of Water and
  Wastewater, published by the American Public Health Association, the American
  Water Works Association and the Water Environment Federation. The testing
  procedures for waste constituents and characteristics shall be as provided in 40
  Code of Federal Regulations 136 (40 CFR 136).

B. Other terms not defined shall be defined as they are in the latest adopted
  applicable editions of the California Codes applicable to building construction.

C. Subject to the foregoing provisions, the following definitions shall apply unless
  the context in which the words or terms are used clearly indicates a different
  intention.

  "Best management practices" (BMP) means schedules of activities, prohibitions
  of practices, maintenance procedures and other management practices to
  prevent or reduce the introduction of FOG to the sewer facilities.

  “Blockage” means a reduction in sewer capacity or impairment of sewage flow.

  "Change in operations" means any change in the ownership, food types, or
  operational procedures that have the potential to increase the amount of FOG
  discharged by FSEs in an amount that creates a potential for SSOs to occur.

  "City Administrator" means the City Administrator of the City of Vernon or his or her
  designee. The City Administrator may delegate a neutral hearing officer to conduct
  any appeal hearing and issue a recommended final decision on the City
  Administrator’s behalf.

  "Director" means the Director of Health and Environmental Control of the City of
  Vernon or his or her designee and/or the Director of Public Works or his or her
  designee.

  "Discharger" means any person who discharges or causes a discharge of
  wastewater directly or indirectly to the City sewer infrastructure.

13.25.060. FOG Discharge Requirements.

No FSE shall discharge or cause to be discharged into the sewer system total dispersed
oil and grease in excess of 650 mg/L or any visible floatable oil and grease.

13.25.070. Prohibitions.

The following prohibitions shall apply to all FSEs:

A. No additives may be introduced into an FSE's wastewater systems for the purpose of
  emulsifying FOG, unless a specific written authorization from the Director is obtained.

B. Waste cooking oil may not be disposed into drainage pipes. All waste cooking oils
  shall be collected and stored properly in receptacles such as barrels or drums for
  recycling or other acceptable methods of disposal.

C. Biological additives for grease remediation or as a supplement to interceptor
  maintenance may not be used without prior written authorization from the Director.

D. Wastes from toilets, urinals, wash basins and other fixtures containing fecal
  materials may not be discharged to sewer lines with grease interceptor service.

E. Any waste including FOG and solid materials removed from the grease control
  device may not be discharged to the sewer system. Grease removed from grease
  interceptors shall be wastehauled periodically as part of the operation and
  maintenance requirements for grease interceptors.

13.25.080. FOG Wastewater Discharge Prohibited.

No person shall discharge, or cause to be discharged any wastewater from a FSE
directly or indirectly into the sewer system without first obtaining a FOG discharge
permit pursuant to the ordinance codified in this chapter by January 1, 2030.

13.25.090. FOG Pretreatment Requirements.

Unless granted a conditional waiver, FSEs are required to install, operate and
maintain an adequately sized grease interceptor necessary to maintain compliance
with the objectives of this chapter, subject to the approval of the Director. The grease

13.25.110. Sewer System Overflows (SSOs), Public Nuisance, Abatement
Orders, Cleanup Costs, and Cost Recovery.

A. Notwithstanding any time limits provided elsewhere in this chapter, any person
  who discharges any waste which causes or contributes to a sewer blockage,
  SSO, obstruction, interference, damage or other impairment to the City’s sewer
  facilities or to the operation of those facilities as a result shall be liable for all
  costs arising out of such discharge including abating, cleaning, repairing, and
  remediating the resulting condition, and the owner of the real property from which
  the discharge originated shall be jointly and severally liable for such costs. Sewer
  line blockages, SSOs or other interferences caused, in whole or in part, by FSE
  discharges are hereby declared public nuisances and are the responsibility of the
  FSE and the property owner of the premises from which the discharge originated
  and may be abated as provided in this chapter or in the manner provided in
  Chapter 8.20. The total amount shall be payable within 45 days of invoicing by
  the City.

B. When the Director determines that a discharge of FOG has caused or
  contributed to a blockage, SSO, or other interference with the City’s sewer
  system, the Director may issue a written abatement and cleanup order to the
  FSE and/or property owner. The order may require the responsible party to:

13.25.240 Grease Interceptor Maintenance Requirements.

A. Grease interceptors shall be maintained in efficient operating condition by
  periodic removal of their full content, including wastewater, FOG, floating
  materials, sludge and solids.

B. No FOG that has accumulated in a grease interceptor shall be allowed to pass
  into any sewer lateral, sewer system, storm drain, or public right of way during
  maintenance activities.

C. FSEs with grease interceptors may be required to submit data and information
  necessary to establish the maintenance frequency grease interceptors.

D. The maintenance frequency for all FSEs with a grease interceptor shall be
  determined in one of the following methods:

  1. Grease interceptors shall be fully pumped out and cleaned at a frequency
  such that the combined FOG and solids accumulation does not exceed
  25% of the total liquid depth of the grease interceptor. This is to ensure
  that the minimum hydraulic retention time and required available volume
  is maintained to effectively intercept and retain FOG.
  2. All FSEs with a grease interceptor shall maintain their grease interceptor
  not less than every six months.
  3. The City may mandate periodic cleaning if it finds that a FSE is not
  maintaining a grease interceptor in a manner in compliance with
  subsection (D)(1) of this section. The maintenance frequency may be
  adjusted when sufficient data have been obtained to establish an average
  frequency that will ensure compliance with subsection (D)(1) of this
  section. Based on the actual generation of FOG from a FSE, the
  maintenance frequency may increase or decrease.
  4. A FSE may submit a request to the Director requesting a change in the
  maintenance frequency at any time. The FSE must demonstrate, to the
  Director’s reasonable satisfaction, that the requested change in frequency
  reflects actual operating conditions based on the average FOG

  this chapter. Any person aggrieved by a final written decision of the Director,
  including but not limited to the imposition of any fee, cost, or administrative
  penalty; the grant, denial, conditioning, suspension, revocation, or modification
  of a FOG discharge permit or conditional waiver, may appeal such decision to
  the City Administrator. Civil penalties imposed under 13.25.310 are excluded
  and shall be pursued under the procedures described in 13.25.310.

B. The appellant shall file a written Notice of Appeal with the City Clerk within 15
  calendar days after service of the Director’s decision. The notice shall identify
  the decision being appealed and state the specific grounds for appeal. For
  appeals involving monetary exactions (fees, penalties, or cost recovery), the
  appellant shall either: (1) pay the amount under protest before it becomes due,
  or (2) post a bond or other security acceptable to the City in the same amount,
  to obtain a stay pending the outcome of the appeal. Failure to file timely or
  secure payment constitutes a waiver of the right to appeal.

C. Effect of Appeal; Stay. A timely appeal shall stay the effective date of the
  Director’s decision, except for emergency suspension or cease-and-desist
  orders issued under 13.25.300, or orders expressly designated by the Director
  as necessary to prevent an imminent threat to public health, safety, welfare, or
  the environment. The appellant may request that the City Administrator grant or
  continue a stay for good cause.

D. Scheduling and Notice of Hearing. Within 10 business days after receiving a
  timely appeal, the City shall schedule a hearing before the City Administrator to
  occur within 45 calendar days (or as soon thereafter as reasonably practicable).
  Written notice of the hearing date, time, and place shall be served at least 10

  1. The hearing shall be informal; technical rules of evidence do not apply.

  2. Parties may be represented by counsel, present testimony and

  3. The appellant bears the burden to show, by a preponderance of the
  evidence, that the Director’s decision should be modified or set aside.
  4. The City shall maintain an administrative record that includes the Notice of
  Appeal, all documents considered by the Director, staff reports, exhibits,
  and a recording or transcript of the hearing.

F. Decision and Findings. Within 15 calendar days after the close of the hearing, the
  City Administrator shall issue a written decision with findings of fact and conclusions
  of law affirming, modifying, or reversing the Director’s decision. The decision shall
  be served on the appellant by first-class mail and, when available, by electronic
  mail. If the appeal involves a monetary exaction paid under protest or secured by
  bond, any refund due shall be paid within 30 calendar days of the decision, without
  interest.

G. Finality and Judicial Review. The City Administrator’s decision is the final
  administrative decision of the City. No further appeal lies to the City Council. The
  decision is subject to judicial review by petition for writ of administrative
  mandamus under Code of Civil Procedure section 1094.5. The time to seek
  judicial review is governed by Code of Civil Procedure section 1094.6, if adopted
  by the City; otherwise, the applicable statute of limitations under state law shall
  apply.

H. Failure to Appear. Failure of the appellant or authorized representative to appear
  at the scheduled hearing shall constitute an abandonment of the appeal, and the
  Director’s decision shall become final.

Subject
General Services Agreement with the County of Los Angeles

Recommendation
A. Find that it is commercially unreasonable to rebid the General Services Agreement (GSA) with
the County of Los Angeles in three years as the County is a governmental entity and sole provider
of the desired services; and
B. Approve and authorize the Mayor to execute the proposed GSA with the County of Los
Angeles for a five-year term effective July 1, 2026, through June 30, 2031.

Background
The City of Vernon (City) maintains long-standing agreements with the County of Los Angeles
(County) to perform various municipal functions that are more efficiently managed by County
personnel. As an essential umbrella contract, the GSA provides the City with continued, as-
needed access to miscellaneous public works and municipal services while incorporating
foundational documents, including the Assumption of Liability Agreement of November 14, 1977
(Attachment 2). With the current 2021 GSA set to expire on June 30, 2026, the new GSA
(Attachment 1) ensures a seamless transition and continued access to these services while
maintaining established legal protections and operational standards between both entities.

The new GSA would be effective for a period of five years from July 1, 2026, to June 30, 2031.
While standard practice is to have a three-year term for agreements pursuant to the City’s special
good governance reform contract terms and procedures outlined in Section 3.32.220 of the
Vernon Municipal Code (VMC), it would be commercially unreasonable to rebid the GSA in three
years as the County’s GSA term is typically five years and the County is the sole provider of the
desired services. The extended duration ensures long-term operational stability and reduces the
administrative burden of frequent renewals, thereby enabling the continuation of a unique
partnership that has been significantly beneficial to the City.

By leveraging County resources for specialized tasks, the City maintains operational flexibility
and avoids the overhead costs associated with maintaining full-time internal departments for
occasional needs. This GSA encompasses a variety of services, including bridge design and
maintenance, traffic signal timing, predatory animal control, city ordinance prosecution, and the
collection of direct assessments. This approach ensures that specialized public works, animal
control, and legal services are managed effectively, allowing the City to enhance its operations
as needs evolve.

City Council approval of the GSA is required pursuant to VMC Sections 3.32.030(A) and
3.32.110(B)(3), as costs associated with the contract are estimated not-to-exceed $250,000 and
Council has the authority to approve contracts exceeding $100,000 and to make the finding
referenced above for the five-year term for contracts in excess of the same threshold. The
projected cost is based on the previous agreement expenses. The Public Works Department is
recommending that the City Council approve a five-year renewal of the General Services

Subject
Notice of Completion for Contract No. 20250340 - 55th Street Recycle Center & Nursery –
Perimeter Wall Project
Recommendation
A. Find that the proposed action is categorically exempt under the California Environmental
Quality Act (CEQA) review, in accordance with CEQA Guidelines Section 15303(e)(Fences),
because the project consists of new construction of limited small new facilities;
B. Accept the work of Oppenheimer National as related to City Contract No. 20250340; and
C. Authorize the Director of Public Works to execute and submit the Notice of Completion for the
project to the Los Angeles County Recorder’s Office.

Background
On May 6, 2025, the City Council awarded City Contract No. 20250340 - 55th Street Recycle
Center & Nursery – Perimeter Wall Project to Oppenheimer National, in the amount of
$388,224.90 plus a 10% contingency amount of $38,822.49. This project involved the
construction of an 8-foot-tall steel perimeter fence and the installation of drought-tolerant
landscape at the front of the property.

On March 3, 2026, the City Administrator approved Change Order No. 1, authorizing additional
time and funds for the proposed work of a 12-inch continuous curb beneath the perimeter
wrought-iron fence to contain stormwater runoff, reducing fence panel spacing from 6 inches to
4 inches, and installation of keypads. The additional $37,691.08 in funding increased the total
construction cost to $425,915.98. Consequently, the change order revised the completion date
from February 7, 2026, to March 4, 2026.

City Contract No. 20250340 was completed and accepted on March 4, 2026, in accordance with
the project plans, specifications, and City Staff expectations.

The Notice of Completion was approved as to form by the City Attorney’s Office.

Fiscal Impact
There is no fiscal impact associated with this report.

Meeting Date:  April 21, 2026
From:  Todd Dusenberry, General Manager of Public Utilities
Department:  Public Utilities
Submitted by:  Adriana Ramos, Principal Management Analyst

Subject
Amendment No. 1 to the Services Agreement with Jacobs Engineering Group Inc.

Recommendation
A. Pursuant to Vernon Municipal Code Sections 3.32.220(B) and 3.32.110(B)(3), find that it is
commercially unreasonable to rebid the agreement for environmental compliance services as the
current vendor, Jacobs Engineering Group Inc. (Jacobs) has already initiated the lengthy process
of revising and updating critical facility permits for the Utility with the South Coast Air Quality
Management District (SCAQMD); and
B. Approve and authorize the City Administrator to execute Amendment No. 1 to the Services
Agreement with Jacobs for environmental compliance services, in substantially the same form
as submitted, to extend the agreement to June 30, 2027 at no additional cost.

Background
Vernon Public Utilities (VPU) serves as an essential resource to the City's business and
residential community, providing dependable, high-quality utility services at competitive rates.
VPU offers electricity, water, natural gas, and fiber-optic services to businesses and residents in
Vernon at lower costs than neighboring utility providers.

All utility services provided by VPU are regulated and permitted by various agencies, including
the South Coast Air Quality Management District (SCAQMD), Los Angeles County Sanitation
Districts (LACSD), Los Angeles Regional Water Quality Control Board (RWQCB), California
Energy Commission (CEC), the California Air Resources Board (CARB), the U.S. Environmental
Protection Agency (USEPA), California State Water Resources Control Board (SWRCB), and
the Department of Toxic Substances Control (DTSC).

On June 6, 2023, the City Council approved a Services Agreement with Jacobs for environmental
compliance services for a total amount not to exceed $1,465,686. The term of the Agreement
between the City and Jacobs is July 1, 2023 through June 30, 2026. In accordance with Vernon
Municipal Code (VMC) Section 3.32.080, Jacobs was selected following the City’s purchasing
procedures and principles of good governance in contracting.

Jacobs is currently working with staff to revise Station A's permit (Facility 14502) to allow the
continued operation of the two 5.75 MW simple-cycle natural gas turbines, known as Gonzales
Units. This permit revision must be completed by the end of the calendar year to ensure the
Gonzales Units can operate beyond 2026.

Additionally, VPU has implemented improvements to the Gonzales Units, and the permits must
be updated to reflect enhanced operational efficiency. Without these revisions, the Gonzales
Units may not successfully pass the source test scheduled for November 30, 2026. On March
24, 2026, Jacobs also assisted with a preliminary source test, which will aid in the permit revision
process. While staff does not have an estimated processing time from SCAQMD for the permit
revision, it is expected to take at least several months.
  .
  .
  Item 9  Page 1 of 190
 Therefore, VPU staff recommends approving Amendment No. 1 with Jacobs, which extends the
agreement until June 30, 2027, at no additional cost. To date, the City has spent $799,289.37,
leaving a remaining balance of $666,396.63. There are sufficient funds available to cover the
one-year extension through June 30, 2027.

The City’s special good governance reform contract terms and procedures outlined in Section
3.32.220 (B) of the VMC require that all professional service contracts be rebid every three years
unless found commercially unreasonable to do so. Moreover, Section 3.32.110(B)(3) of the VMC
indicates that the City Council has the authority to make such findings for contracts that exceed
$100,000. Accordingly, City Council approval is required for the proposed amendment as the
total value of the contract exceeds $100,000 and the amendment seeks to extend the agreement
for one additional year beyond the initial three-year period. Due to the critical work currently
underway to update permits for the Gonzales Units and preparation for the upcoming source test,
it would be commercially unreasonable to change the vendor mid-process.

Amendment No. 1 has been reviewed and approved as to form by the City Attorney’s Office.

Fiscal Impact
There is no fiscal impact associated with this report.

unarmed security guard services for a total amount not-to-exceed $3,067,821.56 for a three-year
term; and
B. Authorize a contingency amount of ten percent (10%) or $306,782.16 in the event of
unforeseen services and expenses, and grant authority to the City Administrator to issue
amendments for an amount up to the contingency amount, if necessary.

Background
Security services are required at critical City facilities and properties, including City Hall and City
Utility facilities, to deter unauthorized access, theft, attack, vandalism, and loitering, as well as to
report any suspicious activity, such as burglary, tampering, damage, and/or fraudulent activities
associated with City property and interests. Unarmed security guards will recognize and report
emergencies and illicit activities involving City properties.

On April 4, 2023, the City Council approved a three-year Services Agreement with S&S Labor
Force Incorporated, dba JRM (JRM) for unarmed security guard services. The current agreement
with JRM is set to expire on April 30, 2026. As per Vernon Municipal Code (VMC) Section
3.32.080, on March 4, 2026, VPU staff issued a Request for Proposals (RFP) to seek proposals
from qualified firms to provide Unarmed Security Guard Services for the City. The RFP was
advertised on the City’s Planet Bids platform. The scope of work included, but was not limited to,
implementing and enforcing access control security policies and procedures, and providing patrol
services to City buildings, properties, and utility facilities, and to recognize and report security
threats, breaches, and suspicious and unpermitted activities. The scope encompasses
monitoring and reporting information about activities in areas that may impact City buildings,
property, interests, and utility facilities.

A total of 29 proposal packages were received by the March 18, 2026 deadline. A qualified panel
of City staff from multiple departments, thoroughly examined the proposals based on professional
qualifications (50%), cost and fees to the City (30%), references (10%), and responsiveness to
the RFP (10%). The top three proposals underwent a second round of evaluation by another
panel of City staff. Based on the evaluation process, the proposal submitted by Good Guard
demonstrated the strongest combination of expertise, relevant experience, and a comprehensive
approach that was best suited to fulfill the scope of services that were outlined in the RFP. The
proposal submitted by Good Guard received the highest score following the evaluation process
and was therefore deemed the most qualified. Good Guard’s experience providing unarmed
security services for other public agencies supports the protection of the City’s assets, ongoing
infrastructure investments, utility operations, the safety of City staff, maintains public safety, and
the .security of critical utility assets.

 C. INTRODUCTION
Good Guard has thoroughly reviewed this solicitation to ensure full alignment with the
City’s requirements. We understand the City’s need for a security partner capable of
providing uninterrupted coverage while maintaining the highest standards of
professionalism and responsiveness.
Our approach to managing this contract centers on four key pillars: a Dedicated
Management Team, 24/7 Command Center support, rigorous Quality Assurance
protocols, and technology-driven performance management through our TrackTik
platform.
Dedicated Management Team
Our Management Team includes our Chief Security Officer, Project Manager, Vice
President of Operations, Supervisors, HR, and payroll support. They will work closely with
City representatives, holding weekly meetings to review billing, turnover rates, guard
management, and project records to ensure all requirements are met.
24/7 Command Center
Our Command Center operates around the clock, 365 days per year, staffed by trained
dispatchers and scheduling coordinators. The Command Center serves as the backbone
of our operational responsiveness, managing same-day callouts, coordinating emergency
coverage, and serving as a communication hub between field personnel, site supervision,
and City representatives. In the event of a critical incident, the Command Center can
dispatch backup personnel, notify all parties, and coordinate with local law enforcement.
Quality Assurance
Good Guard implements a structured QA program that includes unannounced site
inspections, uniform & equipment checks, post order compliance verification, and direct
feedback collection from client representatives.
TrackTik Technology Platform
Our cloud-based guard management platform, TrackTik, enables real-time officer
tracking, electronic Daily Activity Reports (DARs), and immediate incident reporting. The
system integrates GPS-verified guard tour checkpoints, ensuring patrol coverage is
completed as required. All reports are accessible to City representatives via a secure
client portal, providing full transparency into daily operations and historical performance
data.

 D. GENERAL SCOPE OF WORK
  Good Guard will provide comprehensive unarmed security guard
  services across the City of Vernon's municipal and utility
  facilities, delivering a structured, professional security presence
  tailored to the unique operational demands of each location. Our
  approach recognizes that the City of Vernon requires a security
  partner capable of operating across diverse environments with
  consistency, discretion, and adaptaility.
  Good Guard will deploy two professional unarmed security
  officers at City Hall Monday through Thursday, 6:30 a.m. to 6:00
  p.m. Services will include access control enforcement, visitor
  screening, suspicious activity monitoring and reporting, and
  immediate response coordination with the Vernon Police
  Department as warranted.
  Good Guard will maintain a continuous 24/7 single-officer post
  at the Vernon Public Utilities Power Plant Entrance. Given the
  critical infrastructure nature of this assignment, officers deployed
  here will be selected for their experience in utility and industrial
environments. Services will include strict access control enforcement, monitoring for
unauthorized entry or tampering, documentation of all personnel and vehicle movements.
Good Guard will also provide a single officer at the Soto Yard during all non-regular hours.
Officers assigned to this post will focus on perimeter monitoring, deterrence of
unauthorized access, vandalism prevention, and timely reporting of any incidents or
suspicious activity observed during their watch.
Good Guard will deploy one to two roving patrol officers on a 24/7 basis to monitor
approximately 20 designated points of interest throughout the City of Vernon. Roving
officers will operate a company-provided, patrol vehicle equipped with all required safety
equipment. Patrol routes and checkpoint sequences will be random and managed and
documented through our TrackTik electronic guard tour platform. Patrol coverage will be
flexible with the ability to concentrate resources at specific locations or add additional
roving units as operational priorities shift.
When requested by the City, Good Guard will coordinate confidential investigative and
surveillance services through our licensed private investigator partner. All investigative
work will be conducted by properly credentialed PI-licensed professionals and handled
with strict confidentiality.
Good Guard will assign a dedicated account management team to the City of Vernon
contract, ensuring consistent oversight, rapid response to coverage changes, and
proactive communication. A 24/7 emergency contact line will be maintained at all times,
with field supervisors reachable around the clock.

Geofencing Capabilities
Our Supervisors and Dispatch Officers are able to constantly track our officers through
TrackTik’s geofencing capabilities. TrackTik's geofencing establishes a virtual boundary
around each property we serve, providing live tracking of officer locations throughout their
shift. If an officer leaves the designated perimeter or remains idle for an extended period,
our dispatch team receives an immediate alert and can contact the officer directly. This
ensures full accountability and confirms that coverage remains uninterrupted.
Live Reporting
While on shift, security officers are able to develop detailed Daily Activity Reports (DARs)
in seconds. Each entry captures the officer's name, shift notes, photos or audio, GPS
location, and timestamp. Reports update automatically throughout each shift and can be
scheduled for delivery daily, weekly, or monthly based on the City’s preference. In any
report pulled, each entry will include the reporting guard’s name, shift notes, photos
and/or audio, said guard’s GPS location, and a timestamp. Color-coded entries allow our
dispatch team and client staff to quickly identify and monitor activity types.

Meeting Date:  April 21, 2026
From:  Brian Saeki, City Administrator
Department:  City Administration
Submitted by:  Lilia Hernandez, Assistant to the City Administrator

Subject
Report on Contract Approved by the City Administrator for a Business Tax Contribution Study

Recommendation
Receive and file the report on the Services Agreement with Kosmont & Associates, Inc. for real
estate advisory services related to the analysis of municipal fees and taxes, as approved by the
City Administrator pursuant to Vernon Municipal Code Section 3.32.110(B)(2).

Background
The City’s Utility Users Tax (UUT) generates approximately $14 million each year, which
represents more than 15% of the City’s total revenues, making it the City’s second largest
revenue source. The UUT (Measure R) was passed by voters in 2018 and is scheduled to sunset
in 2028 unless renewed by the voters. In anticipation of the expiration of the UUT, on October
21, 2025, the City Council received a presentation on the potential of placing a measure to extend
the UUT on the ballot for the April 2026 General Municipal Election. Subsequently, a presentation
was also made to the Vernon Business and Industry Commission (BIC) and discussed at a
Business Breakfast event in late 2025. The business community expressed concerns regarding
the parity, or lack thereof, in the tax contributions paid by different business sectors within the
City. It was suggested that the City consider a study to evaluate whether different business types
contribute their fair share in taxes for their use of City infrastructure and services.

Accordingly, on February 12, 2026, the City Administrator engaged the services of Kosmont &
Associates, Inc. (Kosmont) to conduct a business tax contribution study. Kosmont was tasked
with conducting an analysis of municipal fees and taxes paid by the various types of businesses
located in the City and making recommendations for any necessary adjustments to ensure parity
across business sectors. Kosmont was selected based on their expertise in conducting the
research and type of analysis needed, previous work completed to the City’s satisfaction, and
existing familiarity with the City’s financial structure. Based on the contract amount of $35,000,
the agreement with Kosmont would normally be subject to informal selection requirements.
However, given the time-sensitive nature of the study, the City Administrator determined it was
in the best interest of the City to award a contract to Kosmont, without a competitive selection
process, as Kosmont’s existing familiarity with the City enabled the firm to begin work
immediately. Expediency in completing the study is essential to properly budget for Fiscal Year
2026-27 in anticipation of any potential ballot measures that may need to be explored for the
April 2027 General Municipal Election. A report regarding the contract award is provided to City
Council as required by Section 3.32.110(B)(3) of the Vernon Municipal Code.
Fiscal Impact
The fiscal impact is not-to-exceed $35,000. Sufficient funds are available in General Fund, City
Administration Department, Professional Services Account No. 011-010-105-529215 for the
current fiscal year.

Subject
City Council Strategic Plan – Goal Tasks

Recommendation
As part of the City’s Strategic Planning Process, receive a presentation on proposed tasks to
achieve identified City Council goals and provide direction to staff regarding any desired
modifications.

Background
The City of Vernon is undergoing a Strategic Planning Process to shape the City’s future. The
Strategic Plan will provide a clear framework to guide the City’s decision-making and resource
allocation, aligning goals and objectives with community needs and City Council priorities.

To that end, the City’s strategic planning consultant, Kelly Associates Management Group (Kelly
Associates), facilitated a goal setting workshop for City Council during a Special Council Meeting
held on March 3, 2026. The workshop followed the completion of a SWOT analysis (Strengths,
Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats) and three separate community meetings held in
February 2026 to seek input from Vernon residents and the business community. Subsequently,
on March 17, 2026, the City Council received a presentation on City Council priorities and
determined key goals to guide the City’s Strategic Plan (Attachment 1).

On March 17, 2026, the City Council determined its goals to be as follows:
  1. Strengthen City Credibility and Partnerships
  2. Promote Economic Growth and Revenue Generation
  3. Advance Sustainability and Environmental Stewardship
  4. Enhance Community Infrastructure and Facilities
  5. Strengthen Organizational Efficiency and Financial Planning
  6. Optimize Public Utility Operations to Ensure Affordable Services

Considering the six City Council goals identified above, the City’s executive team has developed
specific tasks to help achieve each of the goals. A draft of the tasks will be presented to City
Council at the April 21, 2026 Council Meeting and will include a schedule, associated cost, and
City department assignment for each task. City Council will have an opportunity to provide
feedback regarding each of the tasks and propose desired modifications. Once a table of tasks
is determined, staff will incorporate the detailed table into the City’s Strategic Plan to be
presented to Council for adoption at a future meeting.

Fiscal Impact
There is no fiscal impact associated with this report.

  PRESENTATIONS

  1.  Presentation of the Police Department’s 2025 Police Officer and Employee of
  the Year Awards
  Recommendation: No action required by City Council. This is a presentation only.

  Police Chief Sousa presented the staff report, and the City Council recognized and
  presented certificates to the 2025 Officer of the Year Award recipient, Officer Rafael
  Sepulveda, and the Employee of the Year Award recipient, Dispatcher Jessica
  Davis.

  2.  Arbor Day Proclamation
  Recommendation: Proclaim April 22, 2026, as Arbor Day in the City of Vernon.

  Public Works Director Wall read the proclamation, the City Council proclaimed April
  22, 2026, as Arbor Day in the City of Vernon, and the proclamation was presented
  to Public Works employees who are involved in the maintenance and care of the
  City trees and who are collaborating with Vernon City Elementary School in an
  Arbor Day celebration taking place on April 22, 2026.

  Recommendation: Receive and file the report on the Services Agreement with

  of municipal fees and taxes, as approved by the City Administrator pursuant to
  Vernon Municipal Code Section 3.32.110(B)(2).

  Mayor Pro Tem Ybarra asked for more details on the contract, and City
  Administrator Saeki explained that the services of Kosmont and Associates were
  retained to help the City with the preparation of the Business Fee Parity Project,

  NEW BUSINESS

  12.  City Council Strategic Plan – Goal Tasks
  Recommendation: As part of the City’s Strategic Planning Process, receive a
  presentation on proposed tasks to achieve identified City Council goals and
  provide direction to staff regarding any desired modifications.

  City Administrator Saeki presented the staff report.

  Mayor Pro-Tem Ybarra expressed concerns about funding for the School
  Interventionist position and stated that the funds should be used to fulfill residents'
  requests. She suggested that the school partner with an organization that is
  already receiving funding for tutoring. Mayor Lopez stated that the School
  Interventionist has direct access to the students at the school and that
  transportation could pose an issue for parents in attempting to get the students
  tutoring.

  Council Member Larios said she understood the concerns expressed by Mayor
  Pro Tem Ybarra and that perhaps the amount of funding required could be
  discussed, and asked whether the City Council could obtain more details for
  consideration of a plan. City Administrator Saeki responded that he would forward
  that information to the City Council and asked that, in the meantime, they consider
  leaving the task on the workplan so that it could be considered when the budget is
  presented to the City Council, because it would need to be budgeted should the
  City Council decide to move forward. He reminded the City Council that the task
  was only for the fiscal year. Council Member Merlo asked the City Council to
  consider the City's area and demographics, and said many parents could not afford
  tutoring for their students. Mayor Pro Tem Ybarra asked that the City Council
  consider other options. There was a consensus from the City Council to leave the
  task on the work plan.

  Regarding Task 1.14, Mayor Pro Tem Ybarra inquired whether there was a staff
  portal where staff could provide feedback via a survey to address morale and the
  services provided by the department to employees.

  City Administrator Saeki informed the City Council that an anonymous survey was
  conducted by a consultant to assess city-wide issues and that changes had been
  implemented as a result.

  Mayor Pro-Tem Ybarra questioned whether staff would control the cost of service
  to businesses as it relates to Task 3.10 – Transitioning to an Exclusive Franchise
  Agreement (EFA) for waste haulers. She stated the cost of service to businesses
  was the primary reason why the transition had not occurred. City Administrator
  Saeki responded that the City would control that; however, there was no guarantee
  that it would be less expensive than the business's current waste haulers.
